questions.stem: A 34-year-old client with heavy menstrual periods reports fatigue and shortness of breath on stairs. The hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL with small, pale red cells. Which other findings fit iron deficiency anemia?

options.text: Spoon-shaped nails, a craving for ice and a low ferritin
A smooth, beefy red tongue with numbness in both of the feet
Yellow sclera, dark urine and an enlarged spleen
Ruddy skin and itching after a hot shower

rationale.correct: Iron deficiency: microcytic anemia, low ferritin, fatigue, pallor, koilonychia and pica.

perOption.a: Low iron stores reduce hemoglobin production and cause koilonychia and pica.
perOption.b: These suggest vitamin B12 deficiency.
perOption.c: These suggest hemolysis.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with iron deficiency anemia is starting ferrous sulfate 325 mg twice a day. The client also takes calcium carbonate for heartburn. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: "Take it with orange juice and expect dark stools."
"Take it together with your calcium antacid each time."
"Stop taking it if your stools turn dark or black."
"Take it with a cup of tea to settle your stomach."

rationale.correct: Oral iron: take with vitamin C, separate from dairy and antacids, use a straw for liquid forms, expect dark stools and prevent constipation.

perOption.a: Vitamin C improves absorption, and dark stools are harmless.
perOption.b: Calcium and antacids reduce iron absorption.
perOption.c: Dark stools are expected with iron.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old client with pernicious anemia received monthly vitamin B12 injections for 3 months and feels much better. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll need these shots for the rest of my life."
"I can stop the shots now that I feel better."
"The tingling in my feet may keep getting better."
"I'll keep going for my follow-up blood tests."

rationale.correct: Pernicious anemia: lack of intrinsic factor means lifelong B12 replacement by injection or high-dose oral or nasal forms, if prescribed.

perOption.a: Lack of intrinsic factor is permanent.
perOption.b: B12 replacement is lifelong because the client cannot absorb it from food.
perOption.c: Neurological symptoms can improve with treatment.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach about lifelong vitamin B12 therapy.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old client who had a gastric bypass 10 years ago has a hemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL with large red blood cells. Which finding suggests vitamin B12 deficiency rather than iron deficiency?

options.text: Tingling of the feet and an unsteady gait
Thin, spoon-shaped nails on both hands
A strong craving to chew ice cubes
A low serum ferritin on the latest tests

rationale.correct: B12 deficiency causes a macrocytic anemia with neurological signs; it is common after gastric surgery.

perOption.a: B12 is needed for nerve function, so neurological symptoms point to B12 deficiency.
perOption.b: This suggests iron deficiency.
perOption.c: Pica suggests iron deficiency.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Tell B12 deficiency apart from iron deficiency.

questions.stem: A clinic nurse is reviewing four clients' histories. Which client is at highest risk for folic acid deficiency anemia?

options.text: A 52-year-old who drinks about a liter of vodka a day and eats little
A 30-year-old vegetarian who eats leafy green vegetables daily
A 28-year-old who is 20 weeks pregnant and takes a prenatal vitamin daily
A 40-year-old who runs marathons and eats a varied diet

rationale.correct: Folate deficiency is linked with heavy alcohol use, poor diet, pregnancy without supplements and some drugs such as methotrexate.

perOption.a: Alcohol impairs folate absorption, and the diet is often poor.
perOption.b: Leafy greens are rich in folate.
perOption.c: Prenatal vitamins contain folic acid.
perOption.d: This is not a main risk.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify risk factors for folate deficiency.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old client with sickle cell disease is admitted in vaso-occlusive crisis with pain of 10 out of 10 in the back and legs. The SpO2 is 93%. Which interventions are the priority?

options.text: IV fluids, oxygen and prompt IV opioids for the pain
Cold compresses applied to the painful legs and back
Fluid restriction to reduce strain on the heart
Delaying opioids to reduce the risk of addiction

rationale.correct: Sickle cell crisis: hydration, prompt pain control, oxygen if needed, warmth and treatment of triggers.

perOption.a: Hydration reduces sickling, oxygen treats hypoxemia, and severe pain needs prompt opioids.
perOption.b: Cold causes vasoconstriction and more sickling.
perOption.c: Dehydration worsens sickling.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize care in sickle cell crisis.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a 17-year-old client with sickle cell disease how to prevent crises. Which factors should the client avoid? Select all that apply.

options.text: Dehydration during sports or hot weather
Untreated infections
Mountain trips at high altitude
Swimming in cold water
Drinking plenty of water every day
Getting the yearly influenza vaccine

rationale.correct: Prevent crises by staying hydrated and warm, avoiding low oxygen, keeping vaccines current and treating infections early.

perOption.a: Low fluid volume increases sickling.
perOption.b: Infection increases metabolic demand and sickling.
perOption.c: Low oxygen triggers sickling.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach prevention of sickle cell crises.

questions.stem: A client with sickle cell disease admitted 2 days ago for a pain crisis now has new chest pain, a fever of 38.7 °C, a cough and an SpO2 of 88%. The chest x-ray shows a new infiltrate in the right lower lobe. Which complication does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Acute chest syndrome
Expected crisis pain
Opioid-induced sedation
Iron overload

rationale.correct: Acute chest syndrome: chest pain, fever, hypoxia and a new infiltrate; it needs oxygen, antibiotics, pain control, incentive spirometry and possibly transfusion.

perOption.a: This life-threatening complication needs urgent treatment.
perOption.b: Hypoxia with a new infiltrate is not simple crisis pain.
perOption.c: This does not explain fever and an infiltrate.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old client with sickle cell disease has had four pain crises this year and has started hydroxyurea to reduce them. Which laboratory test is most important for the nurse to monitor during treatment?

options.text: Complete blood count
Fasting lipid panel
Thyroid function tests
Routine urinalysis

rationale.correct: Hydroxyurea increases fetal hemoglobin but can cause myelosuppression; monitor the CBC.

perOption.a: Hydroxyurea suppresses the bone marrow.
perOption.b: This is not the main concern.
perOption.c: This is not the main concern.
perOption.d: This is not the main concern.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client in septic shock is oozing blood from IV sites and has new petechiae. The platelets are 40,000/mm3, the fibrinogen is low, the PT and aPTT are prolonged, and the D-dimer is high. The client has no history of bleeding problems. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Disseminated intravascular coagulation
Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
Hemophilia A
Vitamin K deficiency

rationale.correct: DIC: low platelets and fibrinogen, prolonged PT and aPTT and a high D-dimer; treat the cause and replace blood products.

perOption.a: Widespread clotting uses up platelets and clotting factors, causing bleeding.
perOption.b: ITP lowers platelets but does not cause low fibrinogen and a high D-dimer.
perOption.c: Hemophilia is inherited and has normal platelets and fibrinogen.
perOption.d: This prolongs the PT but does not lower platelets or fibrinogen.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client has received IV heparin for 6 days for a pulmonary embolism. The platelet count has dropped from 240,000 to 95,000/mm3, and the client has a new swollen, painful left leg. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Stopping all heparin, flushes included, and starting argatroban
Increasing the heparin rate to treat the new clot in the left leg
Giving a platelet transfusion to raise the count back up
Switching from IV heparin to subcutaneous enoxaparin

rationale.correct: HIT: platelets fall by more than 50% after 5 to 10 days of heparin; stop all heparin and use argatroban or another non-heparin anticoagulant.

perOption.a: This suggests heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which carries a high risk of clotting.
perOption.b: More heparin worsens HIT.
perOption.c: Platelets may worsen clotting in HIT.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client receiving chemotherapy has a platelet count of 18,000/mm3. Which bleeding precautions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use an electric razor
Use a soft toothbrush
Avoid intramuscular injections
Hold pressure 5 minutes after needle removal
Take aspirin for headaches
Take temperatures rectally

rationale.correct: Thrombocytopenia: prevent trauma, avoid antiplatelet drugs and watch for bleeding.

perOption.a: This prevents cuts.
perOption.b: This prevents gum bleeding.
perOption.c: IM injections can cause hematomas.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old with hemophilia A has a painful, swollen, warm knee after a minor fall at school. The parent has factor VIII at home. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ice, rest and elevation, and factor VIII as prescribed
Apply a heating pad and encourage walking on the leg to loosen it
Give aspirin for the pain and swelling in the knee
Massage the knee gently to reduce the swelling

rationale.correct: Hemarthrosis: rest, ice, compression, elevation and factor replacement; avoid aspirin and NSAIDs.

perOption.a: This controls bleeding into the joint.
perOption.b: Heat increases bleeding, and weight-bearing worsens the joint.
perOption.c: Aspirin increases bleeding.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage bleeding into a joint in hemophilia.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old client with polycythemia vera has a hematocrit of 58%, a ruddy face, headaches and itching after warm showers. The client had a DVT last year. Which treatment should the nurse expect?

options.text: Therapeutic phlebotomy
Oral iron supplements
Packed red cell transfusion
Strict fluid restriction

rationale.correct: Polycythemia vera: phlebotomy, hydration and watching for clots and bleeding.

perOption.a: Removing blood lowers its thickness and the risk of clots.
perOption.b: These stimulate red cell production.
perOption.c: This raises the red cell count further.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with a hemoglobin of 6.8 g/dL is to receive a unit of packed red blood cells. The unit arrived from the blood bank 10 minutes ago. How should the nurse run the transfusion?

options.text: Slowly for 15 minutes while watching closely, done within 4 hours
Over 8 hours to reduce the risk of fluid overload in the client
As fast as possible so the hemoglobin rises without delay
After keeping it in the unit refrigerator until the client is ready

rationale.correct: Packed RBCs: start slowly, finish within 4 hours and monitor closely, especially at first.

perOption.a: Most severe reactions happen early, and longer infusions raise bacterial risk.
perOption.b: This exceeds the 4-hour limit.
perOption.c: Fast early rates make any reaction worse.
perOption.d: Blood is kept only in the blood bank refrigerator.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Infuse packed red blood cells safely.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old client with heart failure is receiving a second unit of packed red blood cells. Ninety minutes in, the client becomes short of breath, with crackles in both bases and a blood pressure of 172/96 mm Hg. The temperature is unchanged. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload
An acute hemolytic transfusion reaction
A mild allergic transfusion reaction
A febrile non-hemolytic reaction

rationale.correct: TACO: stop the transfusion, sit the client upright, give oxygen and anticipate a diuretic; prevent it by infusing slowly in at-risk clients.

perOption.a: Volume overload with limited cardiac reserve causes pulmonary edema and hypertension.
perOption.b: This causes fever, back pain and hypotension.
perOption.c: This causes hives and itching.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Thirty minutes into a transfusion, a client develops a few hives on the chest and mild itching. The vital signs are unchanged from baseline, and breathing is easy. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop the transfusion and notify the provider
Continue the transfusion at a faster rate to finish it sooner
Discard the unit right away in the biohazard container
Ignore the hives because they are expected with blood

rationale.correct: Every reaction starts with stopping the transfusion; only mild allergic reactions may resume after treatment.

perOption.a: Every reaction starts with stopping the transfusion; a mild allergic reaction may resume after an antihistamine, per the provider.
perOption.b: This could worsen the reaction.
perOption.c: The unit is kept until the provider decides.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a mild allergic transfusion reaction.

questions.stem: A competent client who is a Jehovah's Witness has a hemoglobin of 7.4 g/dL after surgery and declines all blood products. Which option might the nurse discuss with the provider?

options.text: An erythropoiesis-stimulating agent with IV iron
A transfusion anyway, since the hemoglobin is so low
Asking the client's adult children to override the refusal
A platelet transfusion instead of red cells

rationale.correct: Respect the refusal; alternatives include ESAs, iron, volume expanders and blood-conservation techniques.

perOption.a: These raise hemoglobin without a transfusion.
perOption.b: A competent client's refusal must be respected.
perOption.c: Family cannot override a competent adult.
perOption.d: This is also a blood product.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Advocate for alternatives when a client refuses blood.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman is admitted with fever and fatigue. The nurse reviews the complete blood count. For each result, select the interpretation.

options.text: Low
Within normal range
High
Low
Within normal range
High
Low
Within normal range
High

rationale.correct: Know the CBC reference ranges, and follow the facility's values.

perOption.b1:a: Normal is about 12 to 16 g/dL for adult females.
perOption.b1:b: The result is low, not within normal range.
perOption.b1:c: The result is low, not high.
perOption.b2:a: The result is high, not low.
perOption.b2:b: The result is high, not within normal range.
perOption.b3:a: The result is within normal range, not low.
perOption.b3:c: The result is within normal range, not high.

references: Laboratory reference ranges as used in common NCLEX review texts; follow the facility's ranges

questions.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease and iron deficiency is to receive IV iron dextran for the first time. The client has never had IV iron before. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give a test dose and watch for anaphylaxis with emergency drugs ready
Push the full dose quickly through the IV to save the client time
Add the iron to the unit of blood the client is also receiving today
Give the full dose without monitoring, since the client has no allergies

rationale.correct: Iron dextran carries a risk of anaphylaxis; newer IV iron products have lower risk but still need monitoring.

perOption.a: Iron dextran can cause anaphylaxis, so a test dose and close monitoring are needed.
perOption.b: Rapid administration is not safe.
perOption.c: Medications are never added to blood.
perOption.d: Monitoring is required even without known allergies.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A 16-year-old with beta thalassemia major has received red cell transfusions every 3 weeks since early childhood for severe anemia. The ferritin is very high, the liver enzymes are rising, and the client has new heart palpitations and fatigue. Which medication should the nurse expect to be prescribed to prevent further damage?

options.text: Deferoxamine
Ferrous sulfate
Warfarin
Vitamin K

rationale.correct: Chelation therapy (deferoxamine or deferasirox) prevents iron overload from repeated transfusions.

perOption.a: Deferoxamine binds excess iron so it can be excreted, protecting the heart and liver.
perOption.b: This adds more iron.
perOption.c: This is not related.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client with septic shock from a perforated bowel is being monitored for disseminated intravascular coagulation. Highlight the findings that suggest DIC.

segments.text: Oozing blood from the IV site and around the arterial line
Petechiae on the chest and arms

rationale.correct: DIC causes clotting and bleeding at the same time.

perOption.s1: Consumption of clotting factors causes bleeding from puncture sites.
perOption.s5: Small clots reduce blood flow to the extremities.
perOption.s7: Fever reflects the sepsis rather than DIC.
perOption.s9: Blood in the urine suggests a coagulopathy.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.
